body: Why would it be warning about that case to begin with? This is a bug report, not a feature request. :+1:
@michaelficarra Maybe, wasn't sure as I don't know the intentions behind `object-shorthand`. But in any case, yes, I don't expect warning here.

More evidence that this must be a bug is that methods can't self-reference but NFEs can. This shouldn't cause a warning:

``` js
!{ a: function a(){ a(); } };
```
@michaelficarra Yeah, likely... but for such case I'd also check for self-reference - if it doesn't exist, then warning should be emitted.
Yeah I think we can say if there is a name it shouldn't warn yeah? I'm fine with that as a geneal exception.
@RReverser Now that would be an enhancement.
I think this is a bug. The intent is to show equivalence, and there is no equivalence here. I'd say just omit warning for any named function expression.

Well, in fact there is definitely equivalence between

``` javascript
{ a() { return 42 } }
```

and

``` javascript
{ a: function a() { return 42 } }
```

So

> but for such case I'd also check for self-reference - if it doesn't exist, then warning should be emitted

(at least as a future improvement)

There's no equivalence there, as

```
{ a() { return 42 } }
```

Is equal to

```
{ a: function() { return 42 } }
```

The function needs to be anonymous for the two to be equivalent.

For now, we should just turn off the warning of the function expression has a name. Going into whether or not the name is used is overkill IMO.

> There's no equivalence there

Not really - according to the spec, the function's `.name` property should be equal to the name of object property, so in runtime same-named function is actually the one equivalent to concise method.

The `name` is not a binding:

```
{ a() { return a; } } // no such identifier "a" - returns undefined
```

vs.

```
{ a: function a() { return a; } } // returns function ref
```

See: https://github.com/johnstonbl01/eslint-no-inferred-method-name
Yes, I know and wrote about this above. I'm talking about runtime equivalent (the `name` property which is often important).

I feel like we are talking in circles.

My point is that we should never warn when a property has a named function expression, as the shorthand version would not behave the same way. It doesn't matter if the name is the same as the property or not, this rule shouldn't warn for it.

If you want something that cares about function expression name being the same or different than the property, then that would be a different rule.

issue.title: Fix: object-shorthand rule should not warn for NFEs (fixes #2748)
